claims.text: A machine-learning phonon-transport model trained on systematically generated first-principles data will reliably identify high-entropy alloys with ultralow phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% over conventional methods.
The proposed approach will enable experimental discovery of advanced thermal-insulation alloys.
The target materials are equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys containing three to six principal elements, such as 3d transition metals.
The target alloys have single- or dual-phase solid-solution microstructures before thermal treatment.
Local chemical complexity, bond lengths, vibrational spectra, and disorder-sensitive descriptors can be used as model inputs for predicting phonon thermal conductivity.
A temperature range of 300–1000 K is relevant to the intended thermal-insulation application.
Short-range disorder and lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys reduce phonon mean free paths.
Reduced phonon mean free paths suppress phonon thermal conductivity.
The model will capture configurational and vibrational complexity by correlating first-principles scattering rates and mode lifetimes with composition and structure.
Current DFT phonon-transport models generally lack systematic machine learning trained on large, compositionally diverse datasets.
The stated limitation of current DFT approaches leads to higher prediction uncertainty for complex multi-element alloys.
The ML approach will have lower average prediction error than traditional theoretical or semi-empirical estimates.
The approach will identify new high-entropy alloys whose measured thermal conductivities are at least 10% below values expected from standard methods.
The approach is primarily applicable to transition-metal or refractory high-entropy alloys with significant configurational disorder.
The approach may not generalize to alloys dominated by electronic or magnonic heat conduction.
The approach may not generalize to alloys containing more than six principal elements.
Unrepresented local structures, off-stoichiometry, and finite-temperature phase changes may reduce predictive performance.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if measured conductivities deviate by more than 20% from ML predictions and the model fails to improve on existing methods.
